details:
**"The Gift of the Magi"**
O. Henry's most famous short story and the near-universal giveaway for him. A poor young married couple, Jim and Della Young, each secretly sacrifice their most prized possession to buy the other a Christmas present, and the gifts end up useless, a classic example of his ironic twist endings.

**Della sells her hair; Jim sells his watch**
The central irony of "The Gift of the Magi." Della sells her long hair to buy Jim a platinum fob chain for his gold watch, while Jim sells that watch to buy Della a set of expensive tortoiseshell combs she can no longer use.

**"One dollar and eighty-seven cents"**
The opening of "The Gift of the Magi," in which Della cries because she has only $1.87 saved to buy Jim a Christmas gift. She later looks at herself in a pier-glass (a tall mirror) before deciding to sell her hair.

**Madame Sofronie**
The owner of the hair-goods shop where Della sells her hair for twenty dollars in "The Gift of the Magi."

**"The Ransom of Red Chief"**
A comic story in which two small-time crooks, Bill Driscoll and Sam Howard, kidnap the son of Ebenezer Dorset, a prominent man in a small town, expecting a big ransom. The boy turns out to be such a terror that the plan backfires completely.

**Ebenezer Dorset and the $250**
The father of the kidnapped boy (Johnny Dorset) in "The Ransom of Red Chief." The kidnappers first demand $2,000, but Dorset counters that they must pay him $250 to take his son back, and they gladly do.

**Old Hank and Snake-eye**
The names Johnny Dorset, who calls himself "Red Chief," gives his kidnappers while playing Indian. He threatens to scalp Bill ("Old Hank") and burn Sam ("Snake-eye") at the stake, and he is first seen throwing rocks at a kitten.

**"The Cop and the Anthem" and Soapy**
A story in The Four Million about Soapy, a homeless man in New York who tries to get arrested so he can spend the winter in jail on Blackwell's Island. All his attempts fail (he is even mistaken for a Yale student celebrating, and keeps an umbrella he thinks he stole), but after hearing church organ music he resolves to reform, and he is then arrested for loitering.

**"The Last Leaf"**
A story set in Greenwich Village in which the young artist Johnsy, sick with pneumonia, believes she will die when the last ivy leaf outside her window falls. The old painter Behrman secretly paints a lifelike leaf on the wall during a storm, saving her, but he dies of pneumonia himself; the leaf was his "masterpiece."

**"A Retrieved Reformation" and Jimmy Valentine**
A story (collected in Roads of Destiny) about the reformed safecracker Jimmy Valentine, who goes straight after falling in love with banker's daughter Annabel Adams. When a child is locked in a bank vault he uses his tools to open it, and detective Ben Price, who came to arrest him, pretends not to recognize him.

**The Four Million**
O. Henry's 1906 collection, titled after the population of New York City at the time (a reply to the idea that only "the Four Hundred" elite people mattered). It contains "The Gift of the Magi," "The Cop and the Anthem," and "The Furnished Room."

**Cabbages and Kings**
O. Henry's only novel, a set of linked stories set in the fictional Central American "banana republic" of Anchuria (a term he coined in it). Its title comes from Lewis Carroll's poem "The Walrus and the Carpenter."

**William Sydney Porter**
O. Henry's real name. He wrote many stories after serving prison time for embezzlement, and the pen name is said to come possibly from a prison guard or a French pharmacist; he is famous for stories with surprise twist endings.

**"The Clarion Call"**
A story in which detective Barney Woods discovers that his old friend Johnny Kernan murdered a man named Norcross, but hesitates to arrest him because he owes Kernan $1,000. He finally pays the debt with a newspaper reward and makes the arrest.

**"A Municipal Report"**
A story set in Nashville in which the narrator discovers that the cab driver Uncle Caesar killed the brutal Major Caswell to protect the poor writer Azalea Adair. The narrator throws away the coat button that would incriminate Caesar into the river.

**Other stories: "The Duplicity of Hargraves" and "The Cactus"**
In "The Duplicity of Hargraves," an actor studies the mannerisms of the Southern gentleman Major Talbot for a play and secretly gives him $300 while disguised as "Uncle Mose." In "The Cactus," a woman accepts a marriage proposal by sending her suitor a cactus whose Spanish name means "come and take me," which he fails to understand.
